{{Short description|Notation for displaying probabilities}}

[[File:Natural frequency tree.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|Visualising natural frequencies in a natural frequency tree improves understanding. The numbers in the boxes are the natural frequencies, while the numbers next to the branches are the conditional probabilities.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=McDowell |first=Michelle |last2=Jacobs |first2=Perke |date=2017 |title=Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/bul0000126 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=143 |issue=12 |pages=1273–1312 |doi=10.1037/bul0000126 |issn=1939-1455|url-access=subscription }}</ref>]]
A common question in medicine is how likely it is that someone has a disease when they get a 'positive' test result. Because some people without the disease also test positive, not everyone who tests positive has the disease.<ref name=":1" /> Expressing the probabilities using '''natural frequencies''' – absolute counts from a sample showing the [[joint probabilities]] (disease x test result) – makes the question easier to answer.<ref name=":0" /> For example, by stating that 100 out of 10,000 women have breast cancer, 90 out of 100 with breast cancer have a positive [[Mammography|mammogram]] and 990 out of 9,900 without breast cancer have a positive mammogram.<ref name=":1" />

In contrast, people struggle when you give the same information as [[Conditional probability|conditional probabilities]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gigerenzer |first=G. |date=2011-10-17 |title=What are natural frequencies? |url=https://www.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/bmj.d6386 |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=343 |issue=oct17 2 |pages=d6386–d6386 |doi=10.1136/bmj.d6386 |issn=0959-8138|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0024-F2A6-A |hdl-access=free }}</ref> That is, when they are given information in a format like this: 80% of women with [[breast cancer]] test positive on a [[Mammography|mammogram]], whereas 9.6% of healthy women also get a positive test ([[False positives and false negatives|false positive]]). One percent of women has breast cancer.<ref name=":1" /> People often neglect the [[base rate]] of people with breast cancer when given this information ([[base rate fallacy]]), leading them to overestimate how likely it is someone has the disease given a positive test result.<ref name=":0" />

In one study, only 6% of medical students could resolve the above question when given probabilities. When the information was presented in natural frequencies instead, 42% gave the correct answer. The students were also twice as fast when using natural frequencies, compared to receiving the information as [[Conditional probability|conditional probabilities]]. Students who received a visualisation of either were more accurate than students who got textual information.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Binder |first=Karin |last2=Krauss |first2=Stefan |last3=Schmidmaier |first3=Ralf |last4=Braun |first4=Leah T. |date=2021 |title=Natural frequency trees improve diagnostic efficiency in Bayesian reasoning |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10459-020-10025-8 |journal=Advances in Health Sciences Education |language=en |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=847–863 |doi=10.1007/s10459-020-10025-8 |issn=1382-4996 |pmc=8338842 |pmid=33599875}}</ref> Similarly, another study found that [[Gynocologists|gynaecologists]] strongly overestimated the chance someone has breast cancer after a positive mammogram.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gigerenzer |first=Gerd |last2=Gaissmaier |first2=Wolfgang |last3=Kurz-Milcke |first3=Elke |last4=Schwartz |first4=Lisa M. |last5=Woloshin |first5=Steven |date=2007-11-01 |title=Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics |url=https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1539-6053.2008.00033.x |journal=Psychological Science in the Public Interest |language=EN |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=53–96 |doi=10.1111/j.1539-6053.2008.00033.x |issn=1529-1006|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0025-7CFC-A |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Similarly, when judging [[DNA profiling|DNA evidence]] in legal contexts, natural frequencies help improve decisions. DNA evidence is not 100% certain, mostly because there is a small chance of a lab error. When provided with natural frequencies, hypothetical jurors made fewer mistakes interpreting DNA evidence, leading to fewer guilty verdicts.<ref>{{Citation |last=Hertwig |first=Ralph |chapter=Technology needs psychology: how natural frequencies foster insight in medical and legal experts |date=2002-08-15 |title=Etc. Frequency Processing and Cognition |pages=285–302 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198508632.003.0018 |access-date=2025-08-08 |publisher=Oxford University PressOxford |isbn=0-19-850863-8 |last2=Hoffrage |first2=Ulrich}}</ref>
